question: What is another name commonly given to the enteric nervous system?
explanation: The enteric nervous system is often called the second brain because it contains a vast network of neurons that can control digestive functions independently of the brain. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h1)

question: When the sympathetic nervous system kicks in during stress, what happens to your digestion?

options.A: It has no effect on the gut

explanation: Think of the 'fight or flight' response—your body focuses on survival, not digesting food, so digestive secretions slow right down. You've got this! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for stimulating the gallbladder to release bile?
explanation: Cholecystokinin is released when fats and proteins enter the small intestine, prompting the gallbladder to contract and release stored bile. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h2)

question: Why does the small intestine release secretin into the bloodstream?

options.A: To neutralize incoming stomach acid with bicarbonate
options.B: To slow down the movement of food through the esophagus
options.C: To stop the liver from producing cholesterol
options.D: To trigger the immediate feeling of hunger

explanation: Secretin is released when acidic chyme arrives from the stomach. It calls for alkaline bicarbonate to protect your delicate intestinal lining—pretty smart teamwork by the body! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h2)

question: What triggers the cephalic phase of digestion?

options.A: The arrival of food in the small intestine
options.B: The sight, smell, or thought of food
options.C: The stretching of the stomach wall
options.D: The absorption of nutrients in the colon

explanation: The cephalic phase is a reflexive response driven by the brain when we sense food through sight, smell, taste, or even thoughts. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h3)

question: Your mouth waters and your stomach rumbles just smelling delicious jollof rice cooking. Which phase of digestion is this?
explanation: That mouth-watering reaction before you even take a bite is your head (cephalic) getting your digestive tract ready for action! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which stomach cells are responsible for secreting hydrochloric acid?
explanation: Parietal cells in the gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid into the stomach lumen. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is the job of pepsinogen once it is inside the stomach?

options.A: It converts into active pepsin to break down proteins
options.B: It lines the stomach wall to protect it from ulcers
options.C: It stimulates the release of bile from the liver

explanation: Chief cells release pepsinogen as a safe, inactive form. Once stomach acid hits it, it turns into active pepsin to start chopping up proteins! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is the primary function of bile salts in digestion?
explanation: Bile salts break large fat globules down into smaller droplets through emulsification, giving digestive enzymes more surface area to act upon. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why does the pancreas send bicarbonate along with its digestive enzymes?

options.A: To break down complex proteins into simple amino acids
options.B: To protect the liver from viral infections
options.C: To stimulate the gallbladder to release stored bile
options.D: To neutralize stomach acid and create the right pH for enzymes

explanation: Stomach acid is very harsh. Bicarbonate acts like a soothing buffer, calming down the acid so the pancreatic enzymes can work safely and effectively. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h5)

question: Which specific cells are responsible for producing protective mucus in the intestinal lining?
explanation: Goblet cells secrete mucus that coats the intestinal lining, shielding it from friction and corrosive digestive juices. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of the watery fluid and mucus secreted inside the small intestine?

options.A: To pump hydrochloric acid into the bloodstream
options.B: To lubricate contents and protect the tissue lining
options.C: To produce hormones that control appetite
options.D: To store bile until fats arrive in the diet

explanation: Think of mucus and fluid as a slippery shield; they keep food moving smoothly while protecting the delicate intestinal walls from irritation. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h6)

question: What usually happens to a patient when their pancreas stops making enough digestive enzymes?

options.B: Severe dehydration from excessive water retention
options.C: Widespread hardening of the intestinal walls
options.D: Rapid weight gain due to unchecked fat storage

explanation: Without enough enzymes, food passes through without being properly broken down, meaning the body misses out on vital nutrients and vitamins. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h7)

question: A doctor prescribes a proton pump inhibitor to a patient with a stomach ulcer. What is the goal of this medicine?

options.A: Reduced stomach acid production to promote ulcer healing
options.B: Increased release of bile to speed up fat digestion
options.C: Stimulation of the vagus nerve to increase appetite
options.D: Enhanced production of mucus by goblet cells

explanation: By shutting down those acid pumps, the stomach environment becomes less acidic, giving the sore tissue a chance to rest and heal up nicely. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h7)
